If you collect Social Security benefits, you're no doubt aware that the program's cost-of-living adjustments, or COLAs, are extremely important. COLAs are what help Social Security benefits keep up with inflation from year to year. And given the number of seniors today who are living on just Social Security benefits, the more generous those COLAs are, the more buying power seniors tend to get. The problem is that Social Security's COLAs have been falling short despite being designed to keep pace with inflation. One proposal seeks to change the way Social Security COLAs are calculated, but whether lawmakers are willing to get on board is a different story. Read More Here › SPONSORED How Social Security COLAs are calculated It used to be that Social Security COLAs had to be voted on by Congress. Now, Social Security benefits are eligible for a COLA automatically each year. Social Security COLAs are based on third-quarter year-over-year changes to the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). When there's an annual increase in the CPI-W, benefits get an increase, too. When the CPI-W stays flat or decreases, benefits stay flat. There are no negative COLAs, so Social Security checks can't decrease from one year to the next. Shopping for cheaper auto insurance? Enter your zip code here to get started. Why Social Security COLAs have been failing seniors The Senior Citizens League reports that Social Security benefits have lost 13.7% of their buying power over the past 10 years. And the reason boils down to insufficient COLAs. The CPI-W may do a good job of measuring cost increases among working Americans. But retirees on Social Security tend to spend their money differently. As such, the CPI-W does not accurately reflect the real-world inflation Social Security recipients experience. Because of this, those annual raises have lagged inflation for seniors despite being tied to an index that measures inflation broadly. A different COLA formula could help The Senior Citizens League specifically flags healthcare as a cost that the CPI-W does not accurately capture. Seniors on Social Security, by nature, tend to spend a larger share of their income on healthcare. And since healthcare costs have risen quickly through the years, Social Security's COLAs have failed to keep up. For this reason, the Senior Citizens League is pushing for COLAs to be based on the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly, or CPI-E. The group says the CPI-E regularly puts spending inflation for seniors at two-tenths of a percentage point higher than the rate by which the CPI-W goes up. That might sound like a small amount. But over a 25-year retirement, it can add up, the group says. In fact, they estimate that a Social Security recipient who retired with an average benefit in 1984 would have received $13,723.16 more through 2011 if the CPI-E had been used to calculate COLAs instead of the CPI-W. Learn More Here › SPONSORED Why lawmakers may not be quick to adopt a new COLA formula It's pretty clear that basing Social Security COLAs on a senior-specific index would help those benefit increases better match inflation as experienced by seniors. The problem is that a change that leads to larger COLAs could push Social Security closer to insolvency. As it is, Social Security is facing the possibility of benefit cuts in the coming years if Congress doesn't implement reforms. Changing the COLA formula could put additional strain on the program's limited resources, making it harder to stave off benefit cuts or, worse yet, accelerating the timeline. Along these lines, the number one priority for Congress right now in the context of Social Security is no doubt to prevent widespread cuts or limit them as much as possible. So it may also be the case that lawmakers simply do not have the capacity to focus on a change to the Social Security COLA formula because they're busy thinking through solutions to prevent benefits from being slashed broadly. If Congress manages to shore up Social Security's finances, at that point, a change to the COLA formula may be more likely to become a point of discussion. Right now, there are bigger problems to deal with. Bottom line Social Security is one of the most important benefits for seniors today. Without those monthly checks, many older Americans would not be able to maintain a reasonable standard of living. The fact that Social Security COLAs have been failing seniors is a problem, though. If those raises can't keep up with real-world inflation, seniors without additional income risk struggling as they get older. While advocates may be pushing to change the Social Security COLA formula, there's no guarantee they'll be successful. So if you're still in the process of planning for retirement, let this be a wake-up call that insufficient COLAs are another reason why it's unwise to retire on Social Security alone. Having additional income streams could help you keep up with rising costs, especially if you hold investments like stocks in retirement that have a history of beating inflation through the years.
